paragraphs: A function is invariant to a group of transformations when applying those transformations leaves its output unchanged. If the target has this property, a neural network can encode it in its architecture. This paper studies the architectural choices available before asking which choice works best for a particular problem.

The authors classify all invariant architectures with one hidden layer and ReLU activations for any finite orthogonal group. Their proof connects transformations of hidden neurons to signed permutations: rearrangements that can also change signs. An equivalent description uses cohomology classes, giving the classification a topological interpretation and identifying architectures the authors believe had not previously been explicitly described.

A second theorem describes inclusion maps between architectures, which could support neural architecture search. The authors also enumerate and visualize architectures for example groups. They prove that architectures from inequivalent cohomology classes coincide in function space only when their weight matrices are zero. Together, these results characterize both the available designs and important distinctions between them within the stated shallow-network setting.
neurips-2022-a-classification-of-g-invar.tldr: The paper classifies symmetry-invariant shallow ReLU architectures and the relationships between them for finite orthogonal groups.

paragraphs: Selecting useful predictors is different from determining how confidently each predictor can be called relevant. This distinction becomes especially difficult in classification when the number of features matches or exceeds the number of samples. The paper addresses statistical inference for sparse logistic regression in this high-dimensional setting.

Its starting point is the Conditional Randomization Test, which can produce p-values while requiring relatively few assumptions about the distribution of its test statistic. The original procedure is computationally expensive. Faster approaches based on distillation exist, but the authors argue that their assumptions are unrealistic and that they have limited power to detect relevant variables.

The proposed CRT-logit algorithm combines variable distillation with a decorrelation step tailored to the geometry of logistic regression with an L1 penalty. This makes the structure of the fitted classification problem central to the testing procedure. The authors provide theoretical analysis and evaluate the method through simulations and large brain-imaging and genomics datasets. These results support its effectiveness as an approach to identifying relevant variables with statistical confidence.
neurips-2022-a-conditional-randomization.tldr: CRT-logit adapts conditional randomization testing to sparse logistic regression through variable distillation and geometry-aware decorrelation.

paragraphs: General value functions let a reinforcement learning agent represent knowledge about both future and past behavior. Applications may require several interdependent quantities to be estimated together using previously collected data from a different policy. This paper examines how to perform that off-policy evaluation accurately with function approximation.

The authors identify a problem with gradient temporal difference learning: estimates can remain substantially wrong even when the approximation class is expressive enough. They develop GenTD through a class of general value functions with causal filtering. The framework covers quantities such as reward variance, value gradients, anomaly-detection costs, and gradients of stationary distributions.

GenTD is shown to learn multiple interrelated, multidimensional value functions as efficiently as a single ordinary scalar value function. Its convergence to the true general value functions is guaranteed when function approximation power is sufficiently large. That condition is central to the result. The contribution combines joint evaluation efficiency with a global optimality guarantee for the studied off-policy framework.
neurips-2022-a-unifying-framework-of-off.tldr: GenTD jointly evaluates interrelated off-policy general value functions, with convergence to the truth given sufficient approximation power.

paragraphs: Recognizing actions in video requires connecting information across frames. Separating spatial processing from temporal processing is computationally efficient, while processing space and time jointly often performs better. The paper attributes this tradeoff to how thoroughly and efficiently a model connects different spatial positions across different frames.

The authors establish that aligning frames has the potential to increase mutual information between their representations, helping retain shared information relevant to the task. Guided by this result, they introduce Alignment-guided Temporal Attention. It extends one-dimensional temporal attention with patch-level alignments between neighboring frames, and those alignments introduce no learned parameters.

The module is designed to plug into image backbones for action recognition without requiring a separate design for each model. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness and general applicability. The theoretical result motivates alignment as a possible way to improve information sharing; the experimental results establish the reported practical benefits. Together, they offer an approach to improving temporal modeling while retaining a broadly usable module.
neurips-2022-alignment-guided-temporal-a.tldr: Alignment-guided Temporal Attention uses parameter-free patch alignment to improve information exchange across video frames.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may need to satisfy several reward objectives at once. The desired compromise can take different forms: balancing rewards fairly, meeting hard constraints, or improving the worst-performing objective. This paper studies policy optimization for Markov decision processes under these different criteria.

The authors introduce Anchor-changing Regularized Natural Policy Gradient, or ARNPG. It is a framework for turning ideas from effective first-order optimization methods into policy optimization algorithms for multiple objectives. The framework therefore provides a systematic route for algorithm design across several ways of combining or constraining reward values, rather than addressing only one chosen tradeoff.

With exact gradients, the resulting algorithms have a global convergence rate of approximately one over the number of iterations, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments also show better performance than some existing policy-gradient approaches, using both exact gradients and sampled information. The distinction matters: the stated convergence rate applies to exact gradients, while the sample-based benefits are empirical. The work connects a general design framework with both theoretical and experimental support.
neurips-2022-anchor-changing-regularized.tldr: ARNPG provides a framework for multi-objective policy optimization with global convergence guarantees under exact gradients.

paragraphs: Blind source separation tries to recover underlying signals from their observed mixtures. Previous biologically plausible algorithms often assumed that the sources were statistically independent or uncorrelated. This paper develops neural algorithms that can instead handle sources that may be dependent or correlated.

The replacement assumption concerns geometry: source vectors must be sufficiently spread throughout domains described by certain polytopes. The authors use a determinant-maximization objective that encourages a similar spread in the recovered signals by maximizing the determinant of their output correlation matrix. Thus, the separation principle relies on the arrangement of source values within an allowed domain.

From this objective, the authors derive two-layer neural algorithms using weighted similarity matching. That approach permits adaptable linear transformations through local learning rules, supporting the intended biological plausibility. The networks accommodate a variety of source domains and outperform other biologically plausible separation algorithms on correlated-source problems. Their contribution is a route beyond independence assumptions, while still relying on explicit geometric conditions for the sources.
neurips-2022-biologically-plausible-dete.tldr: The paper derives biologically plausible networks for separating correlated sources under geometric spread assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies a cloud and a collection of agents learning an unknown function together as data arrive over time. Some agents may be affected by Byzantine attacks, so their contributions cannot all be trusted. The goal is to make federated Gaussian process regression tolerate this source of unreliable information.

The proposed algorithm has three components. Each agent performs local Gaussian process regression, the cloud aggregates information into a cloud-level regression model, and agents perform a further fused regression step. This organization combines learning close to the incoming data with shared estimation and agent-level fusion, making robustness a concern across the collaborative procedure.

The authors derive upper bounds on the error between the cloud model's predicted mean and the target function, provided fewer than one quarter of the agents are Byzantine. They also characterize lower and upper bounds on predictive variance. These results address both prediction error and uncertainty under the stated attack-fraction condition. Experiments on one synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets evaluate the proposed algorithm.
neurips-2022-byzantine-tolerant-federate.tldr: A federated Gaussian process algorithm provides prediction-error bounds when fewer than one quarter of agents are Byzantine.

paragraphs: Fair clustering often uses explicitly observed sensitive attributes to balance the composition of clusters. This paper considers a different information setting: sensitive attributes are not directly available, but an auxiliary graph identifies pairs of nodes that can represent one another with respect to those attributes.

The algorithm receives this representation graph alongside the usual graph of similarities. Its task is to find clusters in the similarity graph while satisfying an individual-level fairness constraint encoded by the representation graph. The authors develop both normalized and unnormalized spectral clustering variants for this setting, incorporating the additional graph into the clustering problem.

They analyze the algorithms under a fair planted partition model in which random similarity graphs depend on both cluster membership and the representation graph. Within that model, they establish consistency results for the constrained procedures, with numerical results supporting the theory. The contribution is a formal connection between an individual-level fairness requirement and clustering performance guarantees under an explicit graph-generating model.
neurips-2022-consistency-of-constrained-.tldr: The paper establishes consistency results for spectral clustering constrained by individual-level fairness encoded in an auxiliary graph.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning separates decisions made over longer periods from lower-level control. As environments become larger and episodes become longer, learning can consume much more data. The paper argues that sharing the episode's overall horizon burdens one or both levels of existing hierarchical approaches.

DHRL addresses this by decoupling the horizons of the high-level and low-level policies. A graph bridges the gap between the lengths of those horizons. This lets the interval between high-level actions stretch, supporting longer temporal abstraction without requiring the two levels to share the same effective decision horizon.

The authors report faster training in complex tasks and better performance than state-of-the-art hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithms in typical evaluation environments. They also demonstrate long, complex locomotion and manipulation tasks. The significance of the approach is its structural treatment of a scaling problem: it changes the relationship between planning at the high level and control at the low level. The reported results support this design as a way to alleviate data inefficiency in larger environments.
neurips-2022-dhrl-a-graph-based-approach.tldr: DHRL uses a graph to decouple high-level and low-level decision horizons, improving learning on long, complex control tasks.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains one model to handle several tasks, requiring a choice about how their training losses interact. Specialized multi-task optimization methods are often presented as better than ordinary optimization of a weighted average of those losses. This paper tests that claim through large-scale experiments on language and vision tasks.

Across the investigated settings, the specialized methods do not improve performance beyond what traditional optimization approaches can achieve. This finding matters because the specialized algorithms also introduce design and computational complexity. The evidence challenges whether that additional complexity produces a useful performance advantage in the evaluated tasks.

The authors also identify alternative strategies that consistently improve the performance profile and discuss training pitfalls that can lead to poor results. They examine difficulties in evaluating multi-task optimizers reliably and outline potential solutions. The contribution therefore concerns both empirical outcomes and how comparisons should be conducted. Its conclusion is grounded in the tested methods and settings, rather than a proof about every possible multi-task optimization algorithm.
neurips-2022-do-current-multi-task-optim.tldr: Large-scale experiments find no advantage for the tested specialized multi-task optimizers over achievable traditional optimization results.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to learn from several observed distributions and perform well on unseen ones. A common strategy combines training error with a penalty intended to encourage generalization. The paper argues that an inaccurate penalty, or difficulty optimizing both terms together, can needlessly worsen performance on the training distributions.

The authors reverse the relationship between these objectives. They minimize the generalization penalty subject to the requirement that empirical risk remain optimal. Under this formulation, the penalty cannot impair optimization of empirical risk. This protects the training-distribution objective without requiring the penalty itself to perfectly capture what will generalize.

To solve the constrained problem efficiently, the authors connect it to rate-distortion theory and use tools from that area. They describe the approach as applicable to any penalty-based domain generalization method and demonstrate significant improvements on three examples from prior work. The guarantee concerns preserving empirical-risk optimality; the improvements in domain generalization are demonstrated experimentally. This distinction explains both the method's firm protection and its practical motivation.
neurips-2022-domain-generalization-witho.tldr: The method optimizes a domain-generalization penalty while constraining empirical risk to remain optimal.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models can sometimes produce a correct solution if allowed many attempts. Selecting that solution from the candidates is another problem. Existing approaches often run generated programs against known unit tests, which requires both available tests and a way to execute potentially dangerous code safely.

CodeRanker learns to rank sampled programs by predicted correctness without executing them at selection time. Its training is fault-aware: it predicts execution-related information, including specific compilation or runtime error types such as IndexError and TypeError. This gives the ranking model a more detailed training signal about program failures than an undifferentiated correctness judgment.

The authors report significant improvements in pass@1 accuracy for several code generators, including Codex, GPT-Neo, and GPT-J, on APPS, HumanEval, and MBPP. Here, the benefit concerns the correctness of the single candidate ultimately selected. The results support learned ranking as a way to improve candidate selection when execution-based filtering is impractical. Predicting correctness remains distinct from certifying that a program is correct.
neurips-2022-fault-aware-neural-code-ran.tldr: CodeRanker improves selection among generated programs by learning correctness and fault predictions without executing candidates.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained generative adversarial network from one example is difficult when the target changes more than visual style. A reference can introduce both textures or colors and entities absent from the source domain. This paper addresses both kinds of change using a reference image and a binary mask identifying its entity.

The method constrains differences between internal distributions of the reference image and generated images using sliced Wasserstein distance. An initial style-fixation stage roughly establishes the reference style. An auxiliary network added to the generator helps disentangle entity transfer from style transfer, giving the two changes distinct roles within adaptation.

The authors also introduce variational Laplacian regularization to constrain the adapted generator's smoothness and support correspondence across domains. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate effectiveness in several scenarios. The contribution is a broader one-shot adaptation formulation that explicitly handles new entities alongside global appearance. Its one-shot setting still includes the supplied entity mask, which is part of the information used to guide the transfer.
neurips-2022-generalized-one-shot-domain.tldr: The method adapts a GAN's style and entities from one reference image and its binary entity mask.

paragraphs: Repeated brain scans of the same person contain relationships across both space and time. Treating scans as independent observations overlooks this structure. The paper develops self-supervised learning for longitudinal image analysis, where useful representations should capture anatomy while accounting for subject-specific changes across follow-up scans.

The pretraining method uses local features at multiple image scales and exploits their spatiotemporal self-similarity within a subject. Feature-level regularizations prevent degenerate representations, a problem the authors identify in naive multiscale extensions. During finetuning, a separate self-supervised segmentation-consistency regularizer uses correlations between scans from the same person.

The framework is evaluated on several segmentation tasks involving adult MRI in neurodegenerative settings and developing infant brain MRI. It outperforms well-tuned models trained from random initialization and existing self-supervised approaches designed for independent or longitudinal data. The reported gains include both segmentation performance and longitudinal consistency. Together, the two training stages make repeated observations useful for learning features and for producing more consistent segmentations over time.
neurips-2022-local-spatiotemporal-repres.tldr: Multiscale spatiotemporal pretraining and segmentation-consistency regularization improve longitudinal brain MRI segmentation.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning trains an agent across tasks so it can quickly solve a new task drawn from the same distribution. This paper asks how many training tasks are needed to guarantee approximately optimal expected reward with high probability. The target is behavior optimized for the underlying distribution of tasks.

The proposed approach first estimates that task distribution and then trains a policy using the estimate. Its theoretical bounds depend on the distribution's dimension. When tasks lie on a low-dimensional manifold, the analysis incorporates dimensionality reduction and obtains substantially better bounds than earlier results that depend directly on the numbers of states and actions.

Kernel density estimation supplies the regularization central to the approach. The authors also incorporate that regularization into VariBAD and demonstrate its practical usefulness. The theoretical advantage is tied to exploitable structure in the task distribution, especially low dimensionality. The work therefore links how tasks are distributed to how much training experience is needed, while connecting the analysis to an existing meta-learning algorithm.
neurips-2022-meta-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Estimating the task distribution yields meta-RL guarantees that can improve substantially when tasks have low-dimensional structure.

paragraphs: Semantic correspondence matches related locations across images despite differences in appearance and background. Existing pipelines extract high-level features, but these often produce coarse matching fields that must be interpolated afterward. Neural Matching Fields, or NeMF, aims to represent more precise correspondences directly through an implicit neural representation.

The matching field is four-dimensional because it relates positions in two images. To manage its complexity, a cost-embedding network processes a coarse cost volume and guides a fully connected network that represents the finer matching field. This preserves coarse matching evidence while using a neural representation to establish higher-precision relationships.

Evaluating every possible pair of pixels would still be computationally expensive. NeMF therefore samples matching candidates randomly during training and combines iterative PatchMatch-based inference with coordinate optimization at test time. The authors report competitive results on several standard semantic-correspondence benchmarks. The contribution pairs a continuous matching representation with procedures that make training and querying the high-dimensional field more manageable.
neurips-2022-neural-matching-fields-impl.tldr: NeMF represents visual correspondences implicitly and uses targeted training and inference to handle a high-dimensional matching field.

paragraphs: Why might a learner need a large model when a smaller one could represent a useful solution? This paper investigates whether computational limits can create that gap. It constructs learning tasks where computationally bounded learners require substantially more parameters than learners unconstrained by computation.

The authors further show that robust learning can increase the parameter requirements for computationally bounded learners. Their results extend the question of model size beyond what is possible given information alone. In the tasks they study, the resources available to find a robust solution can impose additional demands on the size of the model used.

The paper also examines whether restricting the attacker's computation can reduce those demands. It demonstrates a task that can be learned efficiently and robustly against a computationally bounded attacker, while robustness against an unrestricted attacker requires significantly more parameters. These are possibility results established through particular tasks. They show that both learner and attacker computation can matter for model size without claiming to explain every successful large model.
neurips-2022-overparameterization-from-c.tldr: Constructed learning tasks show that computational limits can increase required model size, especially for robustness.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to make a trained model forget specified data, but repeated training and removal operations can be costly. PCMU prepares for a series of future removal requests through a one-time operation combining training and unlearning in advance, without knowing which data will later be removed.

The paper connects randomized smoothing used for certified classification robustness with smoothing used for certified unlearning through gradient quantization. Its first framework combines randomized data smoothing and quantized gradients. The authors derive a certified radius describing allowable changes to data and a corresponding certified budget for data removals.

Obtaining high-confidence certificates in that first framework presents a difficulty. The authors therefore introduce a second, practical framework that smooths gradients and quantizes them. They derive a radius for gradient changes, relate it to the data-change radius, and establish a corresponding removal budget. The resulting guarantees are expressed through these certified radii and budgets, making the scope of advance preparation central to the method.
neurips-2022-prompt-certified-machine-un.tldr: PCMU prepares for future unlearning requests using randomized smoothing and gradient quantization with certified removal budgets.

paragraphs: An implicit neural representation stores a continuous signal in a neural network's parameters. Although this can be compact, editing the signal is difficult. Converting it into discrete samples for processing sacrifices its continuous representation. This paper studies how to process such signals directly through the network.

INSP-Net builds processing operators from spatial derivatives of the implicit representation. These derivatives can be computed analytically. The authors show that continuous convolution filters can be uniformly approximated by linear combinations of higher-order differential operators. INSP-Net turns this result into weighted combinations of derivative computation graphs, with weights that can be learned from data.

The authors also build INSP-ConvNet, a convolutional neural network operating implicitly on these representations. Experiments support the expressiveness of both approaches for image and geometry processing, including blurring, denoising, inpainting, and smoothing, as well as image classification on implicit fields. The central contribution is a mathematical and computational route for manipulating continuous neural signals without first explicitly decoding them into a discrete representation.
neurips-2022-signal-processing-for-impli.tldr: INSP-Net processes implicit neural signals directly by learning combinations of their spatial derivatives.

paragraphs: Sequential training data can be incomplete in two ways: labels may lack timing information, and some labels may be missing altogether. Standard sequence losses such as Connectionist Temporal Classification struggle when many labels are absent. Star Temporal Classification, or STC, is designed to learn under both conditions.

STC introduces a special star token into the possible alignments between inputs and labels. Where a token may be missing, the star permits alternatives covering all possible tokens. The loss therefore accommodates unknown portions of the sequence. The authors express the computation using weighted finite-state transducers and use GTN to differentiate through those structures.

In speech-recognition experiments, STC narrows the gap to a supervised baseline to about 1% word error rate with up to 70% of labels missing. This describes a gap to the baseline, not an absolute error rate of 1%. Handwriting-recognition experiments also demonstrate applicability beyond speech. The results support incorporating missing-label possibilities directly into sequence alignment as a useful way to train from incomplete supervision.
neurips-2022-star-temporal-classificatio.tldr: STC uses a wildcard-like star token to train sequence models when labels are missing and unaligned.

paragraphs: Rendering a dynamic scene from new viewpoints requires a representation that changes with the video. This paper uses explicit grids to reconstruct streaming radiance fields efficiently. It treats the video incrementally, allowing the model to adapt as frames arrive instead of fitting one model jointly to the entire sequence.

For each frame, the method learns a model difference that complements adaptation of a base model. A narrow-band tuning strategy makes this incremental process efficient, and an additional optimization strategy further accelerates frame processing. The model differences also provide a basis for compression, reducing the storage overhead associated with explicit grid representations.

On challenging video sequences, the authors report training at 15 seconds per frame while maintaining competitive rendering quality. They report a 1,000-fold speedup over state-of-the-art implicit methods in those experiments. These are training-speed results rather than a claim of real-time frame-rate training. The contribution combines incremental updating, explicit scene representation, and difference-based compression into a framework for processing evolving scenes.
neurips-2022-streaming-radiance-fields-f.tldr: Incremental explicit-grid radiance fields enable fast per-frame training and compressible updates for dynamic-scene rendering.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter search must decide both which configurations to try and how much training to spend on each. Multi-fidelity methods use partial training information to make this allocation more economical. This paper argues that existing approaches still distribute their search budget suboptimally and introduces DyHPO to improve those decisions.

DyHPO uses Bayesian optimization to decide dynamically which feasible configuration should receive more training. Its Gaussian process model includes a learned deep kernel that captures learning-curve dynamics. An acquisition function also incorporates information from multiple training budgets. Together, these components use how configurations develop during training to guide the continuing race for resources.

The authors evaluate DyHPO in large-scale experiments spanning 50 tabular, image, and language datasets, with architectures including multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, neural architecture search settings, and recurrent networks. They report significant superiority over state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimization methods. The findings support learning resource-allocation decisions from evolving training evidence across a broad set of evaluated tasks and model families.
neurips-2022-supervising-the-multi-fidel.tldr: DyHPO uses learning-curve dynamics and multi-budget evidence to decide which hyperparameter configurations deserve further training.

paragraphs: Understanding motion includes following particular points on a surface as an object moves or deforms. Those tracks can support reasoning about shape, physical properties, and interactions. This paper formalizes tracking any point, or TAP, and introduces a benchmark for evaluating it over longer video clips.

TAP-Vid combines real-world videos with accurate human-annotated tracks and synthetic videos with exact ground truth. A semiautomatic crowdsourcing pipeline uses optical-flow estimates to compensate for easier short-term motion, including camera shake. This lets annotators concentrate on harder portions of a video. The authors validate the annotation pipeline using synthetic data.

The paper also introduces TAP-Net, a simple end-to-end point-tracking model. When trained on synthetic data, it outperforms all prior methods evaluated on the new benchmark. The contribution therefore includes a defined task, a way to collect annotations, an evaluation resource, and a working model. Its reported model advantage is specific to the benchmark, while the benchmark supplies a common basis for comparing future point-tracking approaches.
neurips-2022-tap-vid-a-benchmark-for-tra.tldr: TAP-Vid establishes a benchmark for tracking arbitrary surface points and introduces a strong synthetic-data-trained baseline.

paragraphs: A single video of a person rotating can support body reconstruction, but faces and hands occupy relatively few pixels. Their reconstructed detail therefore tends to lag behind the body. TotalSelfScan addresses this by using several monocular self-rotation videos focused separately on the face, hands, and body.

The extra focused recordings provide more detail for these small but important regions. The model represents body parts separately instead of encoding the entire person in one network. It then fuses observations associated with those parts into a unified human model, connecting detailed local capture to a coherent full-body representation.

Once learned, the model can render photorealistic videos from new viewpoints and under new human poses. Experiments show significant improvements in face and hand reconstruction and rendering quality compared with existing methods. The authors describe the additional recording cost as almost negligible relative to a single-video setup. The method's central idea is to improve both the information captured for small regions and the representation used to integrate it.
neurips-2022-totalselfscan-learning-full.tldr: TotalSelfScan combines focused face, hand, and body videos into full-body avatars with improved small-part detail.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model with guidance from a teacher. Much research changes how their outputs are compared, but the input examples also shape what the student learns. This paper asks why some data augmentations, such as CutMix, work better than others during distillation.

The statistical analysis suggests that useful augmentation should reduce the covariance of teacher-student cross-entropy. The authors also propose a practical metric based on the standard deviation of the teacher's mean probability, called T. stddev, and provide empirical justification for it. These ideas connect augmentation quality to measurable statistical behavior during teacher-guided training.

Building on that perspective, the authors introduce CutMixPick, an entropy-based data-mixing augmentation intended to improve CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support their claims and demonstrate considerable performance gains from choosing better augmentation. The covariance criterion is presented as a suggested principle, supported by analysis and experiments. The practical implication is that improving the examples used in distillation can be valuable alongside work on its training objective.
neurips-2022-what-makes-a-good-data-augm.tldr: A statistical analysis links effective distillation augmentation to cross-entropy covariance and motivates the CutMixPick method.
